chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: The 2013 Taper Tantrum and the Rupee Crisis

body.text: In May 2013, a few sentences from the US Fed Chair about slowing bond purchases set off India's worst currency crisis since 1991. The Fed had not changed a single policy. The lesson that shaped Indian policy for the next decade: a country that depends on foreign money to pay its bills is only as stable as the mood of foreign investors, and the fix is to reduce that dependence, not to fight the Fed.

children.text: You met the Taper Tantrum briefly in Chapter 2, as an example of guidance moving markets, and in Chapter 4 when you studied QE. This lesson tells the full story from India's side: why the rupee crashed, how the RBI and a new Governor fought back, and how that playbook was dusted off again in 2026.

markDefs.definition: Gradually reducing the pace of a central bank's bond purchases under QE, rather than stopping them all at once. It is a slowing of stimulus, not a tightening of policy.

children.text: By 2013, the Fed was buying $85 billion of bonds every month under QE3, flooding global markets with dollars. Much of that money flowed into emerging markets like India in search of higher returns.
meant slowly reducing those purchases, not stopping them or raising rates. But markets heard it as the beginning of the end of cheap global money.

body.title: From a Sentence in Washington to a Crisis in Mumbai

events.title: Bernanke's hint
events.description: Testifying to Congress, Fed Chair Ben Bernanke said the Fed could take a step down in its pace of purchases in the next few meetings. The rupee closed that day at 55.46 per dollar.

events.title: Foreign money runs
events.description: After Bernanke outlined a possible tapering schedule at his June press conference, FIIs pulled a net $7.2 billion out of India in June, $5.4 billion of it from the bond market.

events.title: RBI squeezes liquidity
events.description: The RBI raised the MSF rate to 10.25%, 300 basis points above the repo rate, and capped banks' borrowing under the LAF at ₹75,000 crore, to make it costly to bet against the rupee.

events.title: India labelled "Fragile Five"
events.description: Morgan Stanley grouped India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey as economies too reliant on skittish foreign capital.

events.title: Rupee hits a record low of 68.85
events.description: The rupee lost about 3.7% in a single day, its biggest one-day fall, and the Sensex touched an intraday low of 17,448.71.

events.title: Raghuram Rajan takes charge
events.description: On his first day as Governor, Rajan announced a special swap window to attract dollar deposits from Indians abroad.

events.title: The Fed surprises: no taper
events.description: The Fed held its $85 billion monthly purchases. The next day, Mumbai's stock market jumped 3.43% and the rupee strengthened to about 61.83.

events.title: Rajan's first policy
events.description: The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 7.5% to fight inflation, but cut the MSF rate to 9.5%, beginning to unwind the emergency liquidity squeeze.

events.title: Tapering finally begins
events.description: The Fed cut purchases from $85 billion to $75 billion a month. By then, India was far better prepared, and the Sensex ended 2013 at 21,170.68, up about 9% for the year.

body.title: How Far Did the Rupee Fall?
body.prompt: The rupee was at 55.46 per dollar on 22 May 2013 and hit 68.85 on 28 August 2013. By what percentage did the price of one dollar in rupees rise? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (68.85 − 55.46) ÷ 55.46 × 100 = 24.1%. In about three months, a dollar became nearly a quarter more expensive in rupees. Seen the other way, the rupee lost about 19.4% of its dollar value. Oil, electronics, gold and foreign education all became sharply costlier for Indians.

body.title: What Happened to US Bond Yields?
body.prompt: The US 10-year Treasury yield was 1.66% on 2 May 2013 and hit 2.96% on 10 September 2013. How many basis points did it rise?
body.explanation: 2.96% minus 1.66% = 1.30 percentage points = 130 basis points. Higher, safer US yields made emerging market bonds far less attractive, so global investors sold them. That is how talk about US bond purchases translated into selling of Indian bonds and the rupee.

children.text: Why India Was Hit So Hard

The Fed's signal hit every emerging market, but India was among the worst affected, because its own economy had built up weaknesses that made it dependent on the very foreign money that was now leaving.

cells: The deficit hit a record 4.8% of GDP in 2012-13, around $88 billion. India had to attract that much foreign money every year just to pay for its imports.
Indians were buying huge amounts of gold, a major drain on dollars that added nothing to productive capacity.
Much of the deficit was funded by portfolio flows that could leave in days, rather than long-term investment.
Forex reserves fell to around $275 billion in August 2013, not enough to reassure markets that the RBI could defend the rupee for long.
Persistent high inflation eroded confidence in the rupee and limited the RBI's room to cut rates.

body.title: Why Was India a "Fragile Five" Economy?
body.question: Morgan Stanley grouped India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey in 2013. What did these five economies mainly have in common?
options: They all had fixed exchange rates
They all ran large current account deficits funded by foreign capital that could leave quickly
They were all the largest holders of US Treasury bonds
They had all defaulted on their debt
body.explanation: All five relied on foreign investment to fund large current account deficits. When the prospect of tapering made US assets more attractive, that money started leaving, and their currencies fell sharply. The label was about dependence on skittish flows, not about defaults or fixed currencies.

cells: Raised the MSF rate to 10.25% and capped LAF borrowing at ₹75,000 crore
Make rupees scarce and expensive so speculators could not cheaply borrow rupees to buy dollars
Raised gold import duty in steps to 10% and linked imports to exports under the 80:20 rule
Cut dollar demand from gold imports
Opened a swap window for fresh FCNR(B) deposits of at least three years at a subsidised fixed rate of 3.5% a year, plus a window for banks' overseas borrowing
Attract a large, quick inflow of dollars
Began unwinding the MSF squeeze while raising the repo rate
Restore normal liquidity once the rupee steadied, while fighting inflation

stats.label: Raised via swap windows
stats.context: In the three months to 30 November 2013

body.title: Two Ways to Defend a Currency

columns.label: Squeeze rupee liquidity (July 2013)
points: Pushes up short-term rates for everyone, hurting borrowers and growth
Treats the symptom, not the dollar shortage

columns.label: Attract new dollars (September 2013)
points: Rebuilds confidence that the RBI has firepower
Creates future obligations when the deposits mature

body.text: The tantrum happened on words, not action. When the Fed actually began tapering in December 2013, the reaction was mild, because India had narrowed its gold-fuelled deficit, rebuilt reserves and regained credibility under Rajan. The same Fed decision can shake a vulnerable economy and barely touch a prepared one.

children.text: In June 2026, with the rupee at record lows after the West Asia oil shock, the RBI revived the FCNR(B) swap window that Rajan created in 2013. The parallels are striking, but so are the differences.

cells: West Asia conflict, oil near $110, and hawkish Fed and global central banks
About $136 billion, including $127 billion of FCNR(B) deposits
Effective duty raised to 15% on 13 May 2026

body.title: How Much Bigger Was the 2026 Swap Window?
body.prompt: The 2013 swap windows brought in about $34 billion. The 2026 facility brought in about $136 billion. How many times larger was the 2026 inflow? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: $136 billion ÷ $34 billion = 4.0 times. India's reserves also grew from about $275 billion at the 2013 low to a record $785.71 billion in September 2026, roughly 2.9 times larger. India entered its 2026 crisis with far more firepower, which is one reason the rupee fell in a more controlled way.

body.title: Go Deeper: The Bill That Came Due in 2016

children.text: FCNR(B) swaps are not free money. Banks and the RBI promised to return the dollars when the three-year deposits matured. In 2016, a large wave of the 2013 deposits came up for repayment, and some commentators warned of a new rupee shock.

Rajan described the scheme as the least bad option available in 2013. By 2016, India's reserves had grown substantially, and the RBI managed the repayments without disruption. The same question now hangs over the 2026 window: when those deposits mature from 2029 to 2031, will India's external position be strong enough to repay them smoothly?

body.title: Is 2026 Just 2013 Again?
body.scenario: It is September 2026. A friend who remembers 2013 says: "The rupee crashed, the RBI opened an FCNR window, gold duty was hiked, and foreign investors are fleeing. This is 2013 all over again, so I am moving all my money into dollars before the rupee collapses."
body.prompt: How is 2026 similar to 2013, how is it different, and is your friend's plan sensible?
body.modelAnswer: The similarities are real: a sharp rupee fall driven by global forces, heavy foreign selling, an FCNR(B) swap window to attract dollars, and higher gold import duty to cut dollar demand. But the differences matter more. India's reserves are nearly three times larger than at the 2013 low, and the 2026 swap window raised about four times as much. India's bonds are now in major global indices, and domestic investors, through monthly SIPs of over ₹32,000 crore, provide a steady cushion that barely existed in 2013. In 2013 the rupee recovered about 9.5% from its low within weeks once confidence returned. Moving everything into dollars now means buying after a large fall, locking in a potential loss if the rupee stabilises or recovers. A more sensible approach is to hold some international diversification for long-term reasons, and to keep dollar needs, such as fees or travel, planned and spread out, rather than making a panic bet on a currency collapse.

cards.definition: The 2013 market panic after the Fed hinted at slowing QE bond purchases.
Gradually reducing the pace of QE purchases, not stopping them or raising rates.
Morgan Stanley's 2013 label for Brazil, India, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey: large deficits funded by fickle foreign money.
When a country spends more foreign currency on imports and payments than it earns, it must attract foreign capital to fill the gap.
An RBI scheme letting banks swap foreign currency deposits from NRIs into rupees at a subsidised rate, used in 2013 and 2026.
A 2013 rule requiring 20% of imported gold to be used for exports, to curb gold imports.
The RBI's July 2013 move to raise the MSF rate 300 basis points above repo to make rupee speculation costly.

body.description: Read the original testimony that sparked the Taper Tantrum. Notice how carefully worded it is, and how differently markets heard it.

body.title: Apply the 2013 Lessons Today
steps: Look up India's latest current account deficit as a percentage of GDP and compare it with the record 4.8% of 2012-13
Compare today's forex reserves with the roughly $275 billion low of August 2013
Check how much of India's recent foreign inflow has come from FCNR(B) deposits that must be repaid later
Track the USD/INR rate after the next Fed meeting and note whether India reacts more or less than other emerging markets
Review whether your own finances depend on the rupee staying stable, such as foreign fees or dollar loans

points: The 2013 Taper Tantrum was triggered by Fed Chair Bernanke's hint on 22 May 2013 that the Fed could slow its $85 billion monthly QE purchases.
The rupee fell from 55.46 per dollar to a record low of 68.85 on 28 August 2013, as foreign investors pulled billions out of Indian bonds and stocks.
India was a "Fragile Five" economy, with a record current account deficit of 4.8% of GDP, heavy gold imports and reserves near $275 billion.
The RBI first squeezed liquidity by raising the MSF to 10.25%, then Governor Rajan attracted about $34 billion through FCNR(B) and bank swap windows.
When the Fed actually tapered in December 2013, markets barely reacted because India had rebuilt its defences.
The 2026 crisis revived the same playbook on a far larger scale: an FCNR(B) window raising about $136 billion and reserves reaching a record $785.71 billion.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment or foreign exchange advice. Historical figures are rounded and drawn from contemporary reports. The comparison with 2026 reflects data available up to mid-September 2026.
